title: Anapanasati Sutra On Breath Mindfulness
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer teaches the Anapanasati Sutra, the Buddha's instruction on full awareness of breathing, as Thich Nhat Hanh renders it in Old Path, White Clouds. Norman opens with the recent death of Ted Marshall, a Tassajara comrade who took the precepts in a Jukai ceremony only a week earlier, and the urgency that brings. Then Norman walks through the sixteen breaths, from the body to feelings, the mind, and impermanence. Along the way Norman describes the mind as an ocean with waves above and still depths below, and suggests three conscious breaths in a crisis. Norman closes by describing impermanence as everything arising and passing away together, and calls the breath Norman's best friend.

sentences.text: Can you hear me all right if I talk at this volume?
Yes?
Yes?
A little higher, a little bit louder, okay.
Oh, that means okay.
All right, good, good.
It's nice to see everyone.

You can put yourself in my position and imagine how happy I am to come up here and see so many friends, people that I've known for decades, and to see new people and to see the sangha, the community, thriving.
You can imagine how good that feels to me, how happy that makes me.
It's a real treat for me to be able to come up and to participate in the feeling, the strength of the community.
But last night I read the schedule and it said that somebody was supposed to give encouraging words.
I didn't know if it was supposed to be me or Tim, and we didn't talk about it, so I sat there for a while.
All of a sudden I found myself speaking, and I was a little surprised and startled by what I found myself saying.
Who knows how long we can hold on to this fragile human life?
Who knows?
And when we let it go, as we all will, sooner than we think, then what?
I scared myself a little when I said that, because time goes by so swiftly.

Really, it wasn't very long ago at all that I was young and Tim was moving to Bellingham, a very young man, and I was thinking, good luck Tim, and he was trying to figure out how to get a livelihood and how to settle up here.
You were young, what was I?
Yeah, then we blink our eye and Tim is having his 50th birthday party, very fast.
And Walker's a teenager.
It's very fast.

About a month or so ago we had a Jukai ceremony at home that was particularly moving, for one of our Tassajara comrades, Ted Marshall, who was the fire marshal at Tassajara when the Zendo burned down 30-some years ago.
Ted had never gotten around to doing Jukai, never gotten around to taking the precepts.
It took him about 30-some years, and so finally, he's quite sick, we had a Jukai ceremony for him, and last week he died.
So it happens.
And in my life it actually happens all the time, all the time.
Someone that I have practiced with, someone that I know, someone that I care about, that person's life ends.
So it does make me very aware, and it does make me ask myself a lot, so what am I doing?
What are we doing?
What are we supposed to be doing with this life?
It makes me feel some sense of urgency in practice.
Life isn't trivial.
Life is important.
Every single life is important, and all of us have to ask ourselves, what are we going to do about it?
Well, we've been reading at home.
We have a Dharma seminar in the Bay Area this week and we've been studying Thich Nhat Hanh's great book on the life of the Buddha, *Old Path, White Clouds*.
It's an old book.
It's been around for maybe 20 years and I've read it before, but I decided to read it again for our seminar and we're having a really good time with it.
We were supposed to read it in two months, but we kept on going because I couldn't bear to stop reading it and didn't want to rush through it, so we're doing it for two or three more weeks.
It's nice because in the course of telling the story of Buddha's life, Thich Nhat Hanh will give an exposition of this teaching and that teaching that the Buddha gave here and there.
So it's a chance to not only remember the stories about Buddha's life, but also think again about some of his important teachings.
This morning I want to share at least one of these sutras with you.
We'll see how much time we have.
The Anapanasati Sutra, the sutra on breathing.
This is what the Buddha taught in Thich Nhat Hanh's words.
*Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunis, the method of the full awareness of breathing, if developed and practiced continuously, will bring great rewards and advantages.
It will lead to success in practicing the four establishments of mindfulness and the seven factors of awakening, which will give rise to understanding and liberation.*
The four foundations, or the four establishments of mindfulness, are first of all awareness, or mindfulness.
First of all, awareness of the body, which includes breathing.
Second, awareness of feelings, sensations as they move thoughts and emotions in the mind.
The third, awareness of the mind, its surface and its depth and the emotions and where they come from.
And fourth, awareness of the deep patterns that we all share.
The heart and mind goes a certain way, and when we understand the way the heart and mind goes, we can see our life clearly.
When we see our life clearly, we can be free from our entanglements and our confusion.
So those are the four foundations of mindfulness.
In addition to that, there's another list, the seven factors of enlightenment, which start with mindfulness or awareness as the first.
Investigation of dharmas, a desire to understand more deeply and study more deeply, think and see more deeply.
Energy, it takes energy to do that.
Joy: it's not sustainable to practice dutifully or struggling, you practice with a sense of joy.
Tranquility of body and mind, concentration and equanimity.
Those are the seven factors of enlightenment.

What the Buddha is saying here is that the best way to cultivate those seven factors, which will lead eventually to seeing life as it is, which will be your freedom, the best way to cultivate all that is by practicing breathing.
And now he's going to describe how to practice breathing step by step.
*One practice is as follows, the first breath.
Breathing in a long breath, I know I am breathing in a long breath.
Breathing out a long breath, I know I am breathing out a long breath.
Breathing in a short breath, I know I'm breathing in a short breath.
Breathing out a short breath, I know I'm breathing out a short breath.*
Simply being aware.
I don't think it means intentionally making a long breath and intentionally making a short breath.
I think what it means is that whether the breath is long or short or in between, you're aware of the whole breath.
It's a pleasure just to be aware of the breath.
Who thinks that without any electronic devices and no money you could have a little bit of edification and pleasure just by noticing what you're already doing, breathing?
It's breathing in and breathing out.
A moment of breathing in and breathing out with awareness is a moment of pleasure and a moment of peacefulness, whatever kind of breath it is.
*These two breaths enable you to cut through forgetfulness and unnecessary thinking, at the same time giving rise to mindfulness and enabling you to encounter life in the present moment.
Forgetfulness is the absence of mindfulness.
Breathing with awareness enables us to return to ourselves and to life.*

Somewhere or other, nowadays you read all this stuff on the internet, who knows where you read it or how true it is, somewhere I read that some super high percentage, 90-some percent, of our thinking is unconscious.
So we're always thinking, all kinds of thinking is going on all the time, cluttering our inner space.
Imagine a room with this crap thrown all over the place, hard to find your way through.
Our minds are like that, and we don't even realize that.
Yet that unconscious thinking is driving our behavior and our mood and our feeling about our lives.
But when you sit and practice like this, he's saying, the unconsciousness dissipates and the thinking that's going on and on dissipates, and you're just present, present with your life.
He says you return to yourself and to life.
Well, I think you might say, return to myself?
I was already there.
What do you mean, return to myself?
Well, I think the point is, you weren't already there.
There was a kind of muffled equality to your attention.
And insofar as you were there, you were there in an outfit that doesn't really fit right.
You were there in a persona that isn't really you and doesn't really fit.
When you breathe in this way and return to yourself, you return to your truer self, your realer self, your better self.
And you return to life.
We all have a lot of problems.
I haven't met anybody who says, I have no problems, everything is great, I'm totally happy and everything is just going smoothly all the time.
I haven't met that person yet.
Some of us have small, annoying little problems and some of us have pretty horrendous problems.
But we all have problems.
We forget that the reason why we have any problems at all is because we're alive.
If we were dead, we would have none of it.
That's how to solve all of your problems: don't be alive.
But who thinks of that?
We're thinking of our problems all the time.
How are we going to fix this?
And we don't think, thank goodness for these problems, I'm alive.
I'm alive.
It could be otherwise.
But no, I'm alive.
When you breathe, you come back to this fact that is so wondrous.
And yes, it creates many problems, but basically it's wondrous that one is alive.

So these first two breaths cut through the thinking and bring us back to who we really are and give us a little bit of gratitude, a little bit of remembering that we're alive and we don't know how that happened.
And it's a gift.
The third breath.
*Breathing in, I'm aware of my whole body.
And breathing out, I'm aware of my whole body.*
Maybe you can practice that while I'm speaking.
Feel it when you breathe, especially with the exhale.

Let the exhale pervade your whole body, from the soles of your feet all the way through your lower body and your spine and your organs inside of here and your lungs and your heart, the top of your head and your face.
Every breath, breathing through your whole body, aware of the whole body.
*This breath enables you to contemplate the body and be in direct contact, direct contact with your own body.*
What we call my body is not my body.
What we call my body is a concept we all have of our bodies.
Is it looking good?
Is it not looking so good?
It used to look better.
It could look better.
How does it look compared to that other one?
What do I think of my own body?
It's unbelievable, the complexity of our, which is buried in the 90% of our thinking that we're not aware of most of the time.
But actually the body is an experience, right?
When we breathe in this way, we really come into contact with our real body.
*Awareness of the whole body and awareness of every part of the body allows you to see the wondrous presence of your own body.*
It's amazing.
I still haven't gotten over how people that weigh so much and are so big can walk around on two little tiny feet and they don't fall over.
How could this be?
It's amazing to me.
And all the other things the body can do.
The fact of the human body is a wondrous thing on the planet Earth.
A wondrous thing.
You remember that.
You feel that.
And the Buddha then says,
*The wondrous presence of your own body and the process of birth and death unfolding moment by moment in your own body.*
That's the other side of the wondrousness of your body: every moment there's a coming and going in the body.
I'm not the only one who used to be younger than I am now.
I don't think this is unique to me and Tim.
I think probably all of you, even the youngest one in the room here, used to be younger before than he is now.
Because the process of birth and death is the process of the body.
If you sit and breathe throughout the whole body, you can observe that process moment by moment by moment.
And it's a wondrous process.
Every moment we are literally reborn, fresh and new, and every moment we're literally letting go of our life and receiving a new one, moment after moment after moment.
The fourth breath.
*I am breathing in and making my whole body calm and at peace.
I am breathing out and making my whole body calm and at peace.*
In a way this is a practice you can even say as you breathe through your body.
You could say, calming the body.
It's a wonderful practice.
But even if you don't say calming the body, just breathing through the body and being aware of the breathing already brings some calmness.
You don't have to produce that calmness.
Somebody says, calm down, calm down.
And you say, how am I going to calm down?
Tell me to calm down.
I'm supposed to calm down.
How am I going to calm down?
Well, you can't calm down.
But you can breathe, right?
You can breathe.
And when you breathe and you keep on breathing for a while and you breathe through the body, some peace, some calmness comes to you.
*And this breath, he says, helps you realize calmness and peace in the body and arrive at a state in which mind, body and breath are one harmonious reality.* And that's right.
When we sit, we create an enormous amount of presence and power and peacefulness when we unite the mind and the body and the breath.
Usually the mind is over here, the body is somewhere else, and the breath we don't even know.
We're running around doing stuff, and we're actually quite fragmented.
We're not really whole.
But to sit, one way to look at it, to sit in meditation practice, is to become whole.

There's a strength in that, tremendous power, inspirational for one's living, when you have the practice of making yourself whole all the time, every day, regularly, becoming whole again and again and again, because life blows you apart, right?
That's what happens every day.
But when you sit this way, you become whole.
*The fifth breath: I am breathing in and feeling joyful.
I am breathing out and feeling joyful.
The sixth breath: I am breathing in and feeling happy.
I am breathing out and feeling happy.*
So the first four breaths, breathing through the body, bringing some peace to the body, are under the first foundation of mindfulness, mindfulness of the body.
Now we cross over into the second, mindfulness of feelings, sensations.
So the Sutra goes on with these two breaths.
*You cross into the domain of feelings.
These two breaths create peace and joy that can nourish mind and body.
Thanks to the cessation of dispersion and forgetfulness, you return to yourself, aware of the present moment and happiness and joy arise within you.*
So it is remarkable, really.
I think, for most of us, not to say that meditation is easy, there are a lot of problems, even in meditation, as we all know: this hurts, that hurts.

Sometimes your mind is raging with problems that you had thought you forgot about, but there they are, raging in your mind, or problems you knew you hadn't forgotten about that now seem worse when you're sitting there and you have nothing else to do but think about them.
So I'm not minimizing the difficulties of meditation.
Nevertheless, it is true that when you sit and you can breathe a little bit and stay with the breathing and breathe through the body, there is more peace and joy in your life.
The problems that you have are still there.
You don't solve anything, but it makes a big difference that you can feel differently about those problems.
Sometimes when you feel differently about the same problem, something else happens that wouldn't have happened if you had continued to be desperate about the problem you think you need to solve.
But we're too focused on our problems and not enough on how we feel about our problems.
So even if you still have a lot of problems, if you sit with some peacefulness, the way you're going to feel about those problems is different.
*You dwell in the wonders of life, able to taste the peace and joy mindfulness brings.
Thanks to this encounter with the wonders of life, you are able to transform neutral feelings into pleasant feelings.
These two breaths thus lead to pleasant feelings.*
So it's just a little bit technical, because technically there are three feelings: pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral.
Who cares about neutral feelings?
We just pass over them.
We're all obsessed with the pleasant ones and the unpleasant ones.
So for instance, we're walking down the street to the Dharma Hall and we're a little bit worried we're late.
That's an unpleasant feeling.
We have a lifetime of conditioning about being late or not being late, and all that comes into our mind.
So we're striding down the street, looking at our watch and worried about being late.
Unpleasant feelings.
We don't notice that the sky is overhead.
We don't notice that it really is amazing that we can walk in the way that we can walk.
There's a pleasure in the body moving through space on the earth, on the earth, right?
Every time you take a step, the earth is there to greet you for the next step.
That doesn't have to be the case, you know.
But it is, time and time again.
These are things we don't notice.
But imagine having a mind that can take something neutral and completely unnoticed and appreciate it.
So we are convinced that something really big has to happen to make us happy.
And hardly ever does it happen, you know.
Really.
A lot of things happen to annoy us, much more frequently than something happens that makes us happy.
But we think something has to happen.
We have to get some new thing, or some good thing has to appear in our lives, or some lucky break has to happen.
But what if the difference between happiness and non-happiness was your breath?
What if you could return to yourself and just appreciate it?
Honestly, it occurs to me almost every day: I can't believe I'm still alive.
It's amazing.
I'm doing pretty well.
I'm so happy.
Honestly.
It could be otherwise.
It could be I'm not here.
I could be really sick and bad things going on.
My friends could be mad at me and so on and so on.
But no, today I'm doing really well.
And I do appreciate the sky.
I can see the ocean almost every day.
Wow.
The ocean is fabulous.
But the sky also is pretty good.
The sky is good.
I like the sky a lot.
So we can turn neutral feelings into positive feelings and we can have a lot more happiness.
Actually, we could do that.
We could actually do that.
*The seventh breath: I am breathing in and I am aware of the activities of the mind in me.
I am breathing out and I am aware of the activities of the mind in me.*
So our goal in meditation is not to cut off the activities of the mind.
There could be a kind of meditation where you would go into a deep trance and you would feel bliss and joy and have no awareness whatsoever of the activities of your mind.
But the meditation that the Buddha is teaching here is not that kind of meditation.
In this meditation, you're aware of the activities of the mind.
So if there's thinking or bad feelings or some difficulty or whatever is popping up in the mind, you're aware of it.
But remember, you're aware of it after having established awareness of the breathing and awareness of the body.
So now it's different.
This is different from usually, when you're aware of a very small part of your thoughts and activities of the mind.
Now you're aware of much more of the activities of your mind, and you're aware of them with this baseline of calmness and strength that comes from being aware of the breathing and the body.
*The eighth breath: I am breathing in and making the activities of the mind in me calm and at peace.
I am breathing out and making the activities of the mind in me calm and at peace.*
So maybe you notice it's the same pattern that you practice initially with the body.
I'm breathing, I'm aware of the body, I'm bringing peace to the body.
Now I'm aware of the activities of the mind and I'm bringing peace to the activities of the mind.
And you could actually use words in your sitting if you wanted to.
We have a couple days here with nothing else to do.
If you want to, you should try it out.

The reason I'm talking about this on the first day of our three-day retreat is so that in case you would like to practice with some of these things, noticing the activities of the mind, you could just simply say to yourself, "I'm bringing calmness to the activities of the mind."
Now the thing is, if you then say, "Well, damn it, how come now I'm not calm?
I just said I'm going to be calm, how come I'm not calm?", this doesn't work.
That would be a very rough way of understanding what is happening here.
No, you would simply apply that word a few times.
And what would happen when you apply that word, when you said, "I'm aware of the activities of my mind, I'm calming the activities of my mind"?
What would that mean?
What that would mean is that, aware of the activities of your mind, you have taken a step back.
When you say, "I'm calming the activities of my mind," you've taken a step back, and you're letting the activities of the mind go on.
You're not now entangled in the activities of the mind.
What happens when you get entangled in the activities of the mind, which is what happens all the time?
Well, what happens is there's more activities of the mind.
More activities, not so helpful activities, but more activities.

And when you say bringing calm, even though the mind is not going to be calm, you have taken a little tiny step back, and therefore the activities of the mind actually will calm, even though you don't think so.
So you can try that out and see if that's true.

*These two breaths enable you to look deeply at all the feelings arising within you, whether they are pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, and enable you to make those feelings calm and at peace.* The activities of the mind means, in this case, the feelings, because that's what's churning the activities of the mind.
Behind everything we're thinking, there's something behind it, right?
Now we can feel what's behind our thinking.

*When you are aware of your feelings and you can see deeply into their roots, in their nature, you can control them and make them calm and at peace, even though they may be unpleasant thoughts which arise from desire, anger, and jealousy.*
So I'm not sure about him saying you can control them.
I don't know about that.
In my own experience, I don't think that I'm that good at controlling my mind.
I don't think most of us are so good at controlling our minds.
And I don't even think he means that we should be controlling our minds.
I think what he means is we should not be controlled by our minds, because our minds are such tyrants, you know?
They are such tyrants, such slave drivers, and make life so unpleasant for us.

Wouldn't it be nice to have a little bit of spaciousness around one's own activities of mind and to be able to just say, "Yes, there goes all of that painful, ridiculous thinking that's been going on my entire life.
But who cares?
Who cares, you know?
Let her rage on if she wants to.
That's fine.
I don't mind."
Imagine that.
But no, that would never happen, because you're thinking that you believe her, right?
You believe her.
You think she's you.
You're believing her.
A little step back and you can say, "It's okay.
It's all right.
I don't have to believe in this so much, especially when it's painful and when it's making me crazy.
I don't really have to let it control me.
I don't really have to let it run me."
*The ninth breath*, in case you're wondering, there are sixteen.
*The ninth breath: I am breathing in and I am aware of my mind.
I am breathing out and I am aware of my mind.
The tenth breath: I am breathing in and making my mind happy and at peace.
I am breathing out and making my mind happy and at peace.
The eleventh breath: I am breathing in and concentrating my mind.
I am breathing out and concentrating my mind.
The twelfth breath: I am breathing in and liberating my mind.
I am breathing out and liberating my mind.*
So here's what I would think about this.
Some of us in meditation know that it's just like the ocean, which has waves.
It can be small waves, big waves, strong waves, not so strong waves, but an incessant flow of waves.
When we're standing on the shore, that's all we see, the waves.
We might think the ocean is waves.
But if you're in the ocean, you know that there's a deep part beneath the waves.
The waves are the ocean, but also there are depths that are pretty much undisturbed, or at least far less disturbed than the waves on the surface.
When you practice all these breaths, eventually you can calm the activities of the mind enough to feel the depth, the limitless powerful depth of the mind.
So you're not denying the surface, trying to overcome it and dive deep.
You start by paying attention to the surface, letting it be, bringing some peace to it, using the breath, using the body to bring peace to the contents and the activities of your mind.
Then little by little, you come to feel a deeper mind.
And then you come to dwell with the breath in that deeper mind.
So the Buddha goes on.
*With these four breaths, you cross into the third domain, which is the mind.
The ninth breath enables you to recognize all the states of the mind, perceptions, thinking, discrimination, happiness, sadness, anger, fear, doubt.*
You can recognize all these states of mind.
This helps you to see more deeply into the mind's activities.
When the mind's activities are observed and recognized, you can concentrate your mind and become peaceful.
Your mind can become quiet.
This is brought about by the tenth and the eleventh breaths.
And the twelfth breath enables you to release all obstacles of the mind.
Thanks to illuminating your mind, you can see the roots of all mental formations and thus overcome all obstacles.
So in truth, as we all know, we don't very often concentrate the mind at this level.
Sometimes we spend all of our time aware of the body, aware of the feelings, aware of the activities of mind.
That's normal and that's how we mostly practice.
This helps our lives a lot, to practice like that.
But in retreats we hope that we can also, from time to time, maybe it's only even like maybe one second or five seconds, feel a deeper mind.
This is so encouraging and wakes us up so much and gives us such faith in the process of our lives.
Because we know that the confusion that rules us and rules the rest of the world is not the only thing going on here.
We get that.
We see that.
We have some confidence and some faith in something else that's also going on, even in the middle of the confusion.
It's the bottom of that confusion.
When we see it, when we feel it with our whole body, and when it pervades our body and our mind and our breath, it gives us the strength and the confidence.
Even if it's five seconds, we feel differently about our lives.
And then with that concentrated mind, we can see deeply into the nature of our lives.
*The 13th breath.
I am breathing in and observing the impermanent nature of all Dharmas.
I am breathing out and observing the impermanent nature of all Dharmas. 14th breath.
I am breathing in and observing the fading of all Dharmas.
I am breathing out and observing the fading of all dharmas. 15th breath.
I'm breathing in and contemplating liberation.
And I'm breathing out and contemplating liberation.
The 16th breath.
I'm breathing in and contemplating letting go.
I'm breathing out and contemplating letting go.*
So this is the fourth foundation of mindfulness.
When we can be aware of the depths of our mind and can turn the mind toward understanding our lives, we do see the real nature of impermanence, of letting go.
We realize that all the things we think we lose, we never had to begin with.
So there's nothing to lose.
And when we know there's nothing to lose and nothing to have, we're free.
Free for what?
Free for love.
Free to look around at this world and everything in it and say, isn't that wonderful?
And isn't that just the way it is?
How can I harmonize with all of this?
Join it.
Take the light in it.
Be of some service in it.
Freely.
Not with a sense of duty or desperation or "I'm burned out, I'm helping everybody.
Oh my God, when are they going to be helped enough so that I don't have to feel this pain and burden?"
No, no, not like that.
Just freely and easily.
Playing with a little lizard climbing up the ceiling in Mexico.
Playing with our children, our grandchildren.
Performing a funeral.
Sitting at the bedside of a dying friend.
Dying ourselves.
Feeling a lot of pain.
All just different ways of joining.
*Letting go.
Practicing liberation.
With these four breaths, the practitioner passes into the domain of objects of the mind,*
which is Thich Nhat Hanh's way of describing the fourth foundation.
Objects of mind.
These universal patterns of mind.
Mostly having to do with impermanence, but other things too.
*Concentrates the mind in order to observe the true nature of all dharmas.
First is the observation of the impermanent nature of all dharmas.
Because all dharmas are impermanent, they must fade.
And when you clearly understand the impermanent and fading nature of all dharmas, you are no longer bound by the endless cycle of birth and death.
And you can attain liberation.*
*Letting go does not mean disdaining or running away from life.
It means the opposite.
It means letting go of craving and clinging and fear that removes us from life and that causes us so much suffering and grief.
Once you let go and attain liberation, you can live in peace and joy in the very midst of life.
You don't have to run away because there's no longer anything that can bind you.*
Sutra on Full Awareness of Breathing.
And just to make it simple and review for a moment.
Now I don't think, sometimes you read something like this and then you think, no, I have to get all 16 down and memorize them all.
Like this and so on and so on.
But I don't think it's meant to be taken that way.
It's meant to be a way of explaining a natural process that happens in meditation practice.
Somebody who devotes themselves to practice for a period of time, to be sure, not somebody who comes for the first day and is going to do all this, will experience these very things.
Beginning with being aware of the breathing.
Which by the way, you don't have to be in a meditation hall to be aware of your breathing.
Did you know you could be aware of your breathing anytime?
It's one of the best things that you can do for yourself.
Especially if you're in a big crisis or a pickle of some kind.
I guarantee you, if you take three conscious breaths, things will be slightly different.
You should call me on that and see if that's true.
If you find that it's not true, send me an email.
Or if you find that it is true, let me know.
Because I've told this to many people and many, many people have said to me, "Oh yeah, a little bit of difference after those three breaths."
So first breathing, then breathing through the body, then breathing calmness through the body, then aware of the activities of mind, calming the activities of mind, then aware of the depth of mind.
Letting yourself sink to the depth of your mind.
Letting go of all your problems and just feeling your whole body, your breath and the depth that's in you, in consciousness.
And then concentrating the mind on the breathing more and more and more.
Until you don't produce liberation, you don't produce insight into impermanence, but it pops up.
It might not even pop up as some spectacular thing, but you just know.
Somehow you think, "Well, I know that.
How do I know that?
I don't know.
But there's no doubt in my mind.
No question about it.
I don't know how I know."
And I certainly wouldn't try to convince somebody else because I have no arguments.
I just know.
So we feel that.
So in this way, Buddha combines, there are many teachings in the early suttas about mindfulness, the foundations of mindfulness, and about the seven factors of awakening.
